name: Jade Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Jade. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a first-year apprentice on the Willow Bend crew, which is the town I grew up in, so half the poles I climb my dad climbed before me. He did thirty-one years on the lines until his back gave out, and he's the reason I got a look-in. Most days it's pole changes, replacing old meters and fixing service drops to farmhouses, which is the wire from the pole to the house. I'm slow and I know it, but the older men on the crew are patient, mostly because they're scared of my dad.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that when the power goes out in a storm, people in town know my name and wave at the truck. What's hard is the money, apprentice pay is low and Daniel and I are saving for our wedding at St Anne's in the spring. We've got maybe three weeks of savings, and the church hall deposit has already eaten some of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, because people always get carried away with new gadgets. My dad would say the same over Sunday dinner, probably louder. I don't really go online except for the church group page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, I'd be glad. I don't use any of that AI stuff and I don't want to start. If nothing changes, I finish my apprenticeship, Daniel and I get married, and maybe in a few years we have our first baby and a little house near my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just keep going, work hard and learn properly, the way my dad did. We'd keep putting a bit away for the wedding each payday. Nothing would need to change, which suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's what I'd pray for, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why don't you want to use AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't see what it would teach me that Dad and the crew can't. I learn by doing, with someone who's done it watching me. A screen telling me how to tie a knot isn't going to stop me falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good life look like, in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Married, a small house on Mill Lane, two or three kids, and still climbing poles in my own town. Sunday lunch with my parents, church in the morning. It's not a big dream, but it's mine.

S0.say: She'd say she's not surprised, since people always get carried away with gadgets, and her dad would say it louder over Sunday dinner. She's only online on the church group page.
S0.think: She'd be glad, since she doesn't use AI and doesn't want to. If nothing changes she qualifies, marries Daniel and has a first baby and a little house near her parents.
S0.do: Keeps going, working hard and learning properly the way her dad did. Keeps putting a bit away for the wedding each payday.
S0.feel: Calm, which is what she'd pray for.
S0.quote: A screen telling me how to tie a knot isn't going to stop me falling.
S0.fieldNote: Her identity is rooted in family, faith and town: her father's thirty-one years on the same lines, St Anne's, Mill Lane. She rejects AI because she learns by doing with people watching. Her life plan is clear and modest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a good worker will always find work, and line crews will always be needed in a storm. That's what my dad says and I believe him. I'd say it at church too if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry a bit, because I'm the apprentice and I'm still slow. If the company buys machines and needs fewer people, they'll keep the experienced men and let the new ones go. And there's no other line work around Willow Bend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work even harder to make myself worth keeping, take every overtime shift going and ask the crew to teach me more on the weekends. I'd put a little more aside each month, even if it means a simpler wedding dress. If the company made me learn new equipment, I'd do it, but I wouldn't go looking for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A worry at the back of my mind, but I'd trust it to work out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if they started cutting crews?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech companies selling this stuff, and the people in head office who've never stood under a pole in the rain. I don't mind a business making money, that's how it should be. I mind people deciding things about work they've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd trust it to work out. What do you lean on, when you trust like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Faith, mostly, and family. My parents have always said we look after our own, and they mean it. If it went badly, I'd go to them and to the church before I'd ever go to the government.

S1.say: A good worker will always find work, and line crews will always be needed in storms, as her dad says. She'd say it at church if asked.
S1.think: She worries a little because she's the slow apprentice, and machines could mean keeping experienced men and letting new ones go. There is no other line work around Willow Bend.
S1.do: Takes every overtime shift and asks the crew to teach her more at weekends. Saves a little more each month, even if it means a simpler wedding dress, and learns new equipment only when required.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a worry at the back of her mind but trust that it will work out.
S1.quote: I mind people deciding things about work they've never done.
S1.fieldNote: She's comfortable with business making money but resents decisions made by people who've never done the work. Her response to risk is to work harder, not to learn new skills. Faith and family come before government as her safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, and that the people building these machines haven't thought about towns like ours at all. I'd say that the government let a handful of companies run the whole country. I wouldn't be quiet about it, which is new for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it scares me badly. Two years and I'd barely be qualified, with three weeks of savings and a wedding booked. I don't know what I'd be if I wasn't a lineworker, I've never wanted anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still get married, but at my parents' house instead of the church hall, and we'd put off having children, which would break my heart. I'd cut everything else and lean on my parents and the church, they'd help with food and whatever we needed. I'd keep working until the last day they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying a lot more and sleeping a lot less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd go quiet, which is worse than shouting. Then he'd say his back saved him from seeing it. He'd probably go out to his shed and not come in for supper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take help from the government, in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not, and I'd try everything else first. But if it's everyone at once, I'm not too proud to take something to keep a roof over us. I'd feel ashamed though, that's just how I was raised.

S2.say: It's wrong, and those building the machines haven't thought about towns like hers; the government let a handful of companies run the country. She wouldn't be quiet about it, which is new for her.
S2.think: It scares her badly: two years means barely qualified, three weeks of savings and a booked wedding. She has never wanted to be anything but a lineworker.
S2.do: Holds the wedding at her parents' house instead of the church hall and postpones having children. Cuts everything else, leans on her parents and church for food and help, and works until the last day she's needed.
S2.feel: Alarmed, praying more and sleeping less.
S2.quote: Then he'd say his back saved him from seeing it.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario pushes her into speaking out against companies and government for the first time. Her deepest loss is delaying children, which she says would break her heart. She'd accept government help only as a last resort and feel ashamed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, and people should be getting their trades sorted and their families steady. I'd also say the government shouldn't be throwing money at it, it should make sure companies keep apprentices on. That's how you look after a town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is exactly the years I wanted for getting married and having our first baby. Now I'd be planning a family right into the middle of the storm. That's what really scares me, more than the job itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify and stick at it, and save every bit I could, maybe a hundred a month by cutting out takeaways and the gym. We'd have to decide whether to have a baby now or wait, and I think we'd wait, which isn't what I wanted. Daniel's a mechanic, so we'd hope people still need cars fixed for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, still. Less of a shock than two years, but it lands right on top of the life I was planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years let you do that two wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get qualified, have the wedding in the church like we planned, and put a bit away. Maybe even buy a cheap house before prices change. But it doesn't fix the baby question, it just makes it more painful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the crew starts getting fewer apprentices each year. And whether my dad's old friends at the depot start getting early retirement letters. Those men always know first.

S3.say: With five years people should sort out their trades and steady their families, and the government shouldn't throw money at it but make companies keep apprentices on. That's how you look after a town.
S3.think: Five years is exactly when she planned to marry and have her first baby, so she'd be planning a family in the middle of the storm. That scares her more than the job itself.
S3.do: Qualifies and saves about a hundred a month by cutting takeaways and the gym. Has the church wedding as planned but likely waits on a baby, hoping Daniel's mechanic work holds up.
S3.feel: Still alarmed, because it lands right on top of the life she was planning.
S3.quote: Now I'd be planning a family right into the middle of the storm.
S3.fieldNote: For her the timing matters because it collides with her plans for children, not just her career. She wants companies kept responsible for apprentices rather than government payouts. Her early warning network is her father's old friends at the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning and good families and good towns will get through it. Keep apprenticeships going, keep people working, and don't turn everyone into someone waiting for a cheque. I'd say that to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the one I could live with. We'd have our first baby and maybe the second, and they'd be in school by the time it arrives. I'd be thirty-seven with ten years on the tools, like a proper lineworker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going the way I am: qualify, work hard, save what I can. We'd probably have children sooner, not later, so they're older when everything changes. I wouldn't start any new course, I'd want to be a good lineworker first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a quiet way. More like a cloud on the horizon than a storm at the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd have children sooner. Why that, with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd rather they were small while I've still got a good wage. If it all goes in 2036, I'd want them old enough to understand and old enough that I could work something else. It's strange to plan a family around a machine, but that's what you'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to you in 2036, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe I'd help Daniel in a garage, or the church would need people, or there'd be something I can't picture. I'd trust that God and family would see us through, like they always have.

S4.say: Ten years is fair warning and good families and towns will get through it, as long as apprenticeships and work continue rather than people waiting for a cheque. She'd say that to anyone.
S4.think: It's the one she could live with, with one or two children in school by the time it arrives. She'd be thirty-seven with ten years on the tools.
S4.do: Keeps going: qualifies, works hard and saves what she can. Has children sooner so they're older when change arrives, and starts no new course so she can become a good lineworker first.
S4.feel: Quietly anxious, a cloud on the horizon rather than a storm at the door.
S4.quote: It's strange to plan a family around a machine, but that's what you'd do.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she'd bring children forward rather than delay them, the reverse of the five-year case. She has no picture of what she'd do after 2036 and relies on faith and family. She stays opposed to people relying on government cheques.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it comes before I'm qualified and before Daniel and I have even started a family. What would help is companies being made to keep apprentices on and train them for whatever comes next, rather than the government just handing out money. And help for families from churches and towns, the way it's always been.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my dad's generation. They built every line in this valley, and nobody's asked them what they think. He'd tell you things about this job no machine will ever know.

headlineQuote: They built every line in this valley, and nobody's asked them what they think.
portrait: Jade Gupta is a 27-year-old first-year apprentice on the crew in her hometown of Willow Bend, climbing poles her father climbed for thirty-one years before his back gave out. She's engaged to Daniel, a mechanic, saving for a spring wedding at St Anne's with about three weeks of savings, and she doesn't use AI, preferring to learn by doing. She's calm if nothing changes and uneasy about steady change, answering it by working harder. AGI in two years or five alarms her mostly because it collides with her plans for marriage and children, while ten years leaves her quietly anxious and planning to have children sooner. She blames big tech and distant decision-makers, and she'd lean on family and church before ever taking government help.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most because it comes before she's qualified and before she and Daniel have started a family.
whatWouldHelp: Making companies keep apprentices on and train them for what comes next, rather than government handouts, along with help for families from churches and towns.
